recalc_method: OneDrive upload + Excel for the web recalculation on open + File > Create a Copy > Download a Copy readback

canary.method: openpyxl writes formulas with NO cached <v> value, so the uploaded chunk workbooks contain zero cached results. Opening the workbook in Excel for the web from OneDrive recalculates every formula with Microsoft's own web calculation engine; File > Create a Copy > Download a Copy writes those computed values back out as .xlsx. The deterministic canary =1111+2222 in Z1 of EVERY sheet reading back exactly 3333 therefore proves genuine computation -- without recalculation the cell would read back blank (None), since nothing was ever cached. The volatile =NOW() canary is recorded per chunk as corroboration; like the Drive path (and unlike the LibreOffice runner, which converts the same file twice and shows =NOW() differing) a single open yields one timestamp, so now_differs_across_runs is null by design and the deterministic canary is the load-bearing proof. Corroborating this engine specifically: the downloaded package's docProps/app.xml names the application that wrote it, and is recorded verbatim per chunk under app_provenance_per_chunk.

ABS_zero.description: Zero is its own absolute value

ABS_expression_argument.description: Argument can be any expression evaluating to a number

ABS_cell_reference_negative.description: Absolute value of a negative cell reference

ABS_error_propagates.description: Errors in the argument propagate through ABS unchanged rather than being suppressed

FVSCHEDULE_documented.description: Microsoft's documented example: 1 unit of principal compounded at 9%, 11% then 10%
FVSCHEDULE_documented.notes: Microsoft publishes this example (=FVSCHEDULE(1,{0.09,0.11,0.1})) with the result displayed as 1.3309. The documented computation -- principal times the product of (1+rate) over the schedule -- is exact here: 1 * 1.09 * 1.11 * 1.10 = 1.330890 with no rounding, so 1.33089 is asserted at 7 dp rather than the page's 4-dp display

FVSCHEDULE_principal_scaled.description: The schedule is applied multiplicatively to any principal

FVSCHEDULE_empty_cell_is_zero_rate.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: Excel documents empty cells in the schedule as zeros (a 0% period), not as skipped
FVSCHEDULE_empty_cell_is_zero_rate.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'The values in schedule can be numbers or blank cells; any other value produces the #VALUE! error value for FVSCHEDULE. Blank cells are taken as zeros (no interest).' So the blank is a 0% period: 1000 * 1.1 * 1.0 * 1.1 = 1210. An engine that silently skipped the blank would get the same answer here, but an engine that errored on the blank would not -- so this pins the documented 'blank means 0%' rule

FVSCHEDULE_negative_rate.description: A negative rate in the schedule shrinks the principal

FVSCHEDULE_text_in_schedule_error.description: Non-numeric values in the schedule are an error, not a zero
FVSCHEDULE_text_in_schedule_error.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'any other value produces the #VALUE! error value for FVSCHEDULE'. Note this is the opposite of most statistical functions, which ignore stray text in a reference, and it differs from an empty cell, which the same sentence documents as a zero rate

LENB_ascii_string.description: Microsoft's documented example string: byte length of an 11-character ASCII string
LENB_ascii_string.notes: Microsoft's LEN/LENB page uses 'Phoenix, AZ' as its worked example and publishes LEN = 11. The DBCS rule (see the LENB_non_ascii_characters case) cannot change the answer here because every character is single-byte under either reading. NOTE: the current live page now states 'The LENB function is deprecated' and has dropped the DBCS explanation entirely

LENB_empty_string.description: An empty string has zero bytes
LENB_empty_string.notes: No characters means no bytes, under either the DBCS or the non-DBCS rule

LENB_counts_trailing_spaces.description: Spaces are characters and are counted, including leading and trailing ones
LENB_counts_trailing_spaces.notes: Microsoft documents 'Spaces count as characters' for the text argument of LEN/LENB; the string here is two spaces, three letters and three spaces = 8

LENB_number_argument_coerced.description: A numeric argument is converted to its text representation before measuring
LENB_number_argument_coerced.notes: The number 1234 becomes the four-character string "1234", so the byte length is 4 in a non-DBCS default language

LENB_non_ascii_characters.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: two CJK characters, where the byte count depends on the DBCS language rule
LENB_non_ascii_characters.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft's archived LEN/LENB page: 'LENB counts 2 bytes per character only when a DBCS language is set as the default language. Otherwise LENB behaves the same as LEN, counting 1 byte per character', with DBCS listed as Japanese, Chinese (Simplified/Traditional) and Korean. The harness runs under a non-DBCS default locale, so the documented answer is 2 (LEN semantics). An engine that always counts raw UTF-8 or UTF-16 bytes returns 6 or 4 instead -- recording which one each engine does is the point of this case

LENB_propagates_error.description: An error argument propagates instead of being measured
LENB_propagates_error.notes: The argument evaluates to #DIV/0! before LENB sees it, so the error is the result

MIRR_documented_five_years.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 5 years of cash flows, 10% finance rate, 12% reinvestment rate
MIRR_documented_five_years.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 12.61% (the live page displays it rounded to 13%). Independently derived from the documented formula MIRR = (-NPV(reinvest, positives)*(1+reinvest)^n / (NPV(finance, negatives)*(1+finance)))^(1/(n-1)) - 1 with n = 6 values: the reinvested inflows are carried forward at 12% and the single -120000 outflow discounted at 10%; the 5th root of the ratio gives 0.12609413 -> 0.1261 at 4 dp

MIRR_documented_first_three_years.description: Same doc example truncated to the first three years of inflows, which is still a net loss
MIRR_documented_first_three_years.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as -4.80% (displayed rounded to -5%). Same formula with n = 4 values (-120000, 39000, 30000, 21000): the reinvested inflows do not recover the outflow, so the cube root of the ratio is below 1 -> -0.04804466 -> -0.048 at 4 dp

MIRR_documented_reinvest_14pct.description: Same cash flows with the reinvestment rate raised from 12% to 14%
MIRR_documented_reinvest_14pct.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 13.48% (displayed rounded to 13%). Raising only the reinvestment rate raises the future value of the positive flows; recomputing the documented formula gives 0.13475911 -> 0.1348 at 4 dp

MIRR_zero_flow_in_series.description: A zero cash flow is neither an inflow nor an outflow, so it only contributes to the period count
MIRR_zero_flow_in_series.notes: Excel documents that MIRR ignores text, logical values and empty cells in a reference but INCLUDES cells with the value zero. Zero belongs to neither the positive nor the negative NPV; with finance = reinvest = 0.1, the future value of the inflows is 600*1.1 + 700 = 1360 and the compounded present value of the outflow is -1000, with n = 4 values, so (1360/1000)^(1/3) - 1 = 0.10793165 -> 0.1079

MIRR_no_negative_value_div0.description: Excel documents #DIV/0! when values contains no negative (or no positive) number
MIRR_no_negative_value_div0.notes: With no negative cash flow the denominator NPV of the outflows is zero, and Excel documents that MIRR requires at least one positive and one negative value or it returns #DIV/0!

PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_example.notes: Microsoft publishes =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,2) = 0.333 for the data 13, 12, 11, 8, 4, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1. DERIVATION in exact rational arithmetic: PERCENTRANK.INC gives the r-th smallest of n values the rank r/(n-1) counting r from 0, so the smallest scores 0 and the largest 1 (the "inclusive" of the name), with linear interpolation for a value not in the data. Microsoft spells the same arithmetic out on the page for its first row: "0.333, because 3 values in the set are smaller than 2, and 6 are larger than 2; 3/(3+6)=0.333". Three of the ten values are below 2, so the rank is 3/9 = 0.3333... and the default three significant digits give 0.333. Microsoft's page was re-read live on 2026-08-31 at https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/functions/percentrank-inc-function (the /en-us/office/<name>-function-<guid> path was serving Microsoft's 'Sorry, the page you're looking for can't be found' body throughout this batch, and the working path returns an 87 KB stub about half the time, so pages were fetched with retries until the payload exceeded 150 KB).

PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_truncates_not.description: The documented row whose exact value is 5/9 -- the case that distinguishes truncation from rounding
PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_truncates_not.notes: Microsoft publishes =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,4) = 0.555. THIS IS THE SHARPEST CASE IN THE FILE. Five of the ten values are below 4, so the exact rank is 5/9 = 0.55555... To three significant digits that is 0.555 if the significance argument TRUNCATES and 0.556 if it ROUNDS, and Microsoft publishes 0.555 -- so the documented behaviour is truncation. Microsoft's next row is the same test again in the other direction: =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,8) = 0.666, where 6/9 = 0.6666... truncates to 0.666 and would round to 0.667. An engine that rounds instead of truncating produces a plausible-looking number that differs from Excel in the third decimal on the most ordinary inputs imaginable, and only a case whose exact value is a repeating decimal can see it. EXECUTED RESULT -- A SILENT WRONG ANSWER, AND THE HEADLINE FINDING OF THIS BATCH: LibreOffice returns 0.556 on all four pinned builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3), which agree case for case, where Excel documents and publishes 0.555. LibreOffice ROUNDS the result to the significance digits; Excel TRUNCATES it. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the answer is wrong in the third decimal on the most ordinary input imaginable -- a percentile rank of a small integer list. The companion case in this file (rank of 8, exact value 6/9) shows the same split, 0.667 against Microsoft's published 0.666, and PERCENTRANK.EXC's significance-1 row shows it a third time, 0.4 against Microsoft's published 0.3. The corpus's legacy PERCENTRANK file never caught this because every value it asserts is exact at three digits.

PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_two_thirds.description: The documented row whose exact value is 6/9
PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_two_thirds.notes: Microsoft publishes =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,8) = 0.666. Six of the ten values are below 8, so the exact rank is 6/9 = 0.66666..., truncated to three significant digits by the default significance: 0.666, not 0.667. Asserted alongside the 5/9 case because the two together make the truncation reading unambiguous -- a single repeating-decimal row could be dismissed as a typo on Microsoft's page, two cannot. EXECUTED RESULT: LibreOffice returns 0.667 on all four pinned builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3), which agree case for case, against Microsoft's published 0.666. The second of three demonstrations in this batch that LibreOffice rounds where Excel truncates; see the 5/9 case above.

PERCENTRANK.INC_documented_interpolated.notes: Microsoft publishes =PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,5) = 0.583 and explains it as "one-quarter of the way between the PERCENTRANK.INC of 4 and the PERCENTRANK.INC of 8". DERIVATION: 5 sits between 4 (rank 5) and 8 (rank 6), a quarter of the way along, so the exact rank is (5 + 1/4)/9 = 21/36 = 0.58333..., truncated to 0.583.

PERCENTRANK.INC_largest_value_is_one.description: The largest member of the array, which the inclusive definition sends to 1
PERCENTRANK.INC_largest_value_is_one.notes: Nine of the ten values are below 13, so the rank is 9/9 = 1 exactly. This is the end of the range where .INC and .EXC part company (.EXC would give 10/11 here), so it pins which of the two definitions the engine implemented.

PERCENTRANK.INC_significance_below_one.description: A significance of zero, which the page excludes
PERCENTRANK.INC_significance_below_one.notes: Microsoft documents: "If significance < 1, PERCENTRANK.INC returns the #NUM! error value."

PERCENTRANK.INC_empty_array.description: An empty array, which the page excludes -- D20:D25 is deliberately left blank
PERCENTRANK.INC_empty_array.notes: Microsoft documents: "If array is empty, PERCENTRANK.INC returns the #NUM! error value." D20:D25 is deliberately empty; nothing is written into it by design.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#N/A'

VAR.P_documented_population_variance.description: Microsoft's documented breaking-strength example: population variance of ten tool readings
VAR.P_documented_population_variance.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 678.84, alongside VAR.S over the same data as 754.27. Independently derived: mean 1328.6, sum of squared deviations 6788.4, divided by n = 10 = 678.84 (VAR.S divides by n-1 and so gives 754.2667)

VAR.P_ignores_text_in_range.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: the paired case to VARPA -- VAR.P IGNORES text rather than counting it as 0
VAR.P_ignores_text_in_range.notes: Microsoft's VAR.P page is unambiguous where VARPA's is not: 'Empty cells, logical values, text, or error values in the array or reference are ignored.' Data are 1, 2, 3 with mean 2; squared deviations 1+0+1 = 2, divided by n = 3 gives 0.66667 -> 0.6667. The identical range under VARPA gives 1.25, so the two cases together pin down the coercion rule

VAR.P_ignores_logicals_in_range.description: A logical inside a referenced range is ignored, so only the numbers are used
VAR.P_ignores_logicals_in_range.notes: Microsoft documents logical values in a reference as ignored by VAR.P. Data 4 and 8, mean 6, squared deviations 4+4 = 8, divided by n = 2 gives 4

VAR.P_single_value_is_zero.description: One data point has zero population variance
VAR.P_single_value_is_zero.notes: Population variance divides by n, so a single point gives 0/1 = 0

VAR.P_no_numeric_values_div0.description: A range holding only text leaves VAR.P with no data points
VAR.P_no_numeric_values_div0.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: the VAR.P page documents no error condition. Text in a reference is documented as ignored, so n = 0 and the population denominator is zero -- #DIV/0!

readback_artifacts.method: raw xl/worksheets/*.xml <v> strings inspected directly, then compared against Python's float() parse of the same strings
readback_artifacts.float_precision: LOSSLESS -- no normalization applied or needed. Excel for the web writes full IEEE-754 round-trip decimal, up to 17 significant digits, and uses scientific notation for small magnitudes: ROUND(MIRR(...),4) came back as the literal string '0.12609999999999999' and ROUND(MIRR(...),4) = -0.048 as '-4.8000000000000001E-2'. Every such string was verified to parse to the IDENTICAL double as its short form, so float() recovers the exact value and Python's repr renders it back as 0.1261 / -0.048. This is the OPPOSITE of Google Sheets' export, which is LOSSY: it rounds to 10 significant digits (PI() comes back as 3.141592654), genuinely destroying precision. Excel-web values therefore need no rounding fix-up, and none is applied -- the raw parsed double is recorded.
readback_artifacts.errors: Standard OOXML typed error cells: t="e" with the error token as the cached value (#DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #NUM!, #N/A all observed verbatim). Recorded as-is, exactly like the LibreOffice and Sheets runners. No Google-style #ERROR! parse-failure token exists here.
readback_artifacts.date_formatting_of_numerics: UNMEASURED. Sheets applies a date/time NUMBER FORMAT to DATE()/TIME()-style results, which makes openpyxl surface a datetime instead of the serial (normalize_readback_value converts it back). The probe carried NO date or time function -- every one of its 34 result cells came back with number format 'General' and the workbook declares no custom numFmts at all -- so this run cannot say whether Excel-web does the same. normalize_readback_value is still applied on the same terms as every other engine, so a datetime WOULD be handled correctly if one appears; it simply was not exercised here.
readback_artifacts.empty_string_results: UNMEASURED. No probe case returns the empty string, so whether a formula yielding "" round-trips as a blank cell (None) is untested for this engine. values_roughly_equal() already treats an expected "" as satisfied by a read-back None for every engine, so the existing handling applies unchanged.
readback_artifacts.booleans: UNMEASURED AS A RESULT. The probe contains no boolean-returning formula. A boolean INPUT literal did survive as a real typed t="b" cell rather than the text 'TRUE' -- weak evidence that Excel-web would not stringify a boolean the way Sheets' export sometimes does -- but an input is not a computed result and no claim is drawn from it. The _boolean_text_artifact note still fires for this engine if it ever happens.
readback_artifacts.formula_prefix: The _xlfn. storage prefix survives the round trip verbatim: '_xlfn.PERCENTRANK.INC(A2:A11,2)' came back written exactly that way and COMPUTED (0.333), confirming Excel for the web resolves the storage form. This is why the probe chunk uses the DEFAULT xlfn-translated serialization and NOT --plain-names.
readback_artifacts.volatile_now: =NOW() comes back as a RAW FLOAT SERIAL under 'General' format (46266.42749652778), not as a datetime the way Sheets' export renders it, and it carries the ca="1" volatile flag. It is evaluated in the VIEWER'S LOCAL TIME ZONE, not UTC: the probe's serial decodes to 2026-09-01 10:15:35, which is UTC-7 (America/Phoenix), and the package's own docProps/core.xml records dcterms:created 17:13:37Z and dcterms:modified 17:16:41Z -- so 10:15:35 local == 17:15:35Z falls exactly inside the recalculation window. Anything comparing this timestamp to a UTC clock must account for the offset or it will look ~7 hours stale.
